With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 149 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
The new deaths were reported in Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna and Mymensingh divisions, it said.
Since January 1 this year, hospitals across the country have admitted a total of 51,837 dengue patients.
Of them, 48,093 have been discharged after recovery, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Humaiun: Putul's appointment a shame for international organizations
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has described the appointment of recently resigned Saima Wazed Putul to a senior position at the World Health Organization (WHO) as “very unfortunate”, alleging that she lacked the qualifications, experience and expertise required for such a high-level post.
“It was not a surprise. Someone without any credible qualification, any credible expertise, just because she happens to be the daughter of (Sheikh Hasina) so-and-so, was given the appointment,” he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs questioning the appointment.
The state minister described the appointment of Putul, daughter of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, as regional director for Southeast Asia as a “shame” for international organisations and stressed the need for greater seriousness and scrutiny in selecting people for senior positions.
“You need people who can lead the organization. We need to be very serious about these appointments,” Kobir said.
The state minister said Bangladesh would support a candidate with appropriate qualifications in future, mentioning a candidate from the Maldives who, he said, has a good track record and strong credentials.
“We hope that in the near future the organisation will be led by competent people,” he said.
He said international organisations should not appoint individuals simply because they are connected to a particular political family or regime.
“People should not be appointed simply on the grounds of being connected to a family or a regime,” he said, adding that such organisations have important institutional responsibilities and their leadership should have the necessary expertise and credentials.
Referring to the WHO, Kobir said the organisation is highly important and therefore requires people with appropriate professional expertise to lead it.
“If you put any kind of unqualified people in those positions, the outcome for the region and the world is not going to be good,” he said.
The state minister also referred to a candidate from the Maldives, saying he hoped that a person with stronger credentials would be selected for the position in the future.
Kobir said that if irregularities or corruption were involved in appointments, such matters would eventually come to light.
He reiterated that the credibility, experience and expertise of candidates should be carefully examined before making appointments to senior positions in international organisations.
“Someone without credible qualifications, experience and expertise should not be appointed to such a high-level position,” he said.
He said allegations of corruption, manipulation and concealment of information surrounding such appointments would eventually come to light. “The smell of corruption can never be suppressed; it will eventually come out,” Kobir said.
Referring to the WHO, Kobir said the organisation plays a crucial role in global public health, particularly recalling its importance during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Asked how many countries the government is working with to recover the huge amount of money allegedly siphoned out of Bangladesh, Kobir said the government is working with international partners to bring back laundered assets and funds.
“We are working with international partners to recover the assets and money that have been siphoned out,” he said.
He said Bangladesh has already established a partnership with the United Kingdom in this regard.
The government is also in discussions with countries that have legal and forensic expertise to help trace and recover the assets, he said.
“We are determined to bring back the people’s stolen money and assets through legal and diplomatic processes,” Kobir said.
He said the recovered assets should be used for the welfare of people rather than ending up in the pockets of individuals.

item.title: HC upholds death sentence for ex-constable who killed wife over dowry
item.description:
The High Court on Sunday upheld the death sentence handed down by a trial court to former police constable Abdul Alim Sumon for killing his wife in Tangail over dowry.
The court also commuted the death sentence of another convict, Shamim Al Mamun, to life imprisonment.
A High Court bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakraborty and Justice KM Rasheduzzaman Raja delivered the verdict while disposing of the death reference and appeals filed against the trial court’s judgment.
Senior lawyer SM Shahjahan and lawyers Md Jahangir Alam and KM Al Fahad Bin Sagir appeared for the convicts.
According to the case documents, Abdul Alim, who was serving with the Industrial Police at the time, married Sumi Akter, daughter of Sultan Ahmed of Faliarghona village in Tangail Sadar upazila, on May 6, 2011.
The agreed dowry was Tk5 lakh, but Sumi’s father paid Tk3 lakh, leaving Tk2 lakh unpaid. Alim allegedly subjected his wife to frequent physical abuse over the remaining amount and eventually sent her to her parents’ home.
On April 20, 2012, Alim took Sumi from her parents’ home on the pretext of visiting the Bangabandhu Bridge area. He later took her to the embankment area near Turag in Dhaka, where he allegedly strangled her with a scarf with the assistance of Shamim Al Mamun. After his arrest, Alim confessed to the killing in a statement before a court.
Sumi’s mother later filed a case with Tangail Police Station against the two accused. Alim was subsequently dismissed from the police force.
Following the trial, the Tangail Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal, then presided over by Judge Khaleda Yasmin, sentenced both accused to death on August 5, 2019.
The death reference was later sent to the High Court, while the convicts filed criminal and jail appeals challenging the verdict.

item.title: The succession question returns to haunt Awami League
item.description:
A name has suddenly surfaced across Bangladeshi social media and various established media outlets, a name well known in political circles but one that had not been mentioned publicly for quite some time.
Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim has not only returned to the spotlight, but his name has also sparked a genuine debate both within and outside his party.
This debate was initiated by Sheikh Hasina herself.
In a telephonic interview with the Indian online news portal The Wall, Hasina remarked that Sheikh Selim could assume responsibility for the party in her absence.
Although she described this as a temporary measure in accordance with the party’s constitution, many interpreted it as a sign that she had chosen Sheikh Selim as her successor.
This assumption gave rise to various speculations, such as the idea that Sheikh Hasina was stepping away from politics or retiring, or that she had realized a return to Dhaka was no longer possible and was therefore handing over responsibility to Sheikh Selim.
The actual context, however, was different.
Amal Sarkar, executive editor of The Wall, had raised the issue during the interview. He asked who would take charge of the party if Sheikh Hasina were to be imprisoned or taken into custody by an agency for interrogation upon her return to Dhaka.
In response, Sheikh Hasina explained the Awami League’s constitution, stating that the most senior member of the Presidium would assume responsibility in such a scenario.
Currently, of the 16 Presidium members, three have passed away, six are in prison, one’s whereabouts are unknown, and six remain active. Among them, Sheikh Selim is the most senior.
The explanation is clear. A similar situation arose during the 2007-08 “1/11” government era when Sheikh Hasina was imprisoned.
At the time, senior Presidium member Zillur Rahman took charge. That did not mean he had been designated as Hasina’s successor to the party presidency.
While the matter appears straightforward, there is no doubt that the mention of Sheikh Selim’s name fuelled the subsequent rumours and speculation.
Sheikh Selim has been elected to the National Parliament nine times. This fact alone sends a clear message about his popularity and local influence in Gopalganj.
He is the nephew of Bangladesh’s founding leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, specifically, Sheikh Hasina’s paternal cousin.
Perhaps because of this close familial relationship, many view Sheikh Selim not merely as someone who could take “temporary charge,” but as a potential permanent successor. That is precisely where the complication lies.
A Dhaka-based news portal has already reported that several senior leaders currently in Kolkata held a meeting and expressed disagreement with Hasina’s decision.
The report further stated that they proposed Jahangir Kabir Nanak for the role.
The issue here is that some observers have questioned the credibility of the report, even raising doubts about whether such a meeting actually took place.
Regardless, one thing is clear: There is no unanimous support for Sheikh Selim among Awami League leaders and activists.
Many perceive him as the kind of leader who “disappears during times of crisis.” And this is not merely about Sheikh Selim; the episode signals a deepening crisis within the Awami League.
The reported meeting is merely an indication of how acute the infighting among the party’s leaders in exile has become.
Ever since Sheikh Hasina’s tenure began, this question has been raised repeatedly, yet no satisfactory answer has ever emerged.
Who comes after Sheikh Hasina? Who will take the helm of the Awami League if Hasina retires? Does she have any plans regarding succession?
There has never been a direct answer to these questions.
Whenever confronted with this question, Hasina would say that the party would decide who its leader should be.
However, no one considered the possibility that the party might not be in a position to make such a decision when the time came.
By closing off the path to a transfer of power through elections, the Awami League perhaps believed it could safely remain in power for the long haul.
Yet, having enjoyed the comforts of governance for so long, the party, once a force that shook the streets, forgot that there are far more perilous paths to a change of power than elections.
It was precisely through such a perilous path that it was forced to relinquish power in 2024.
Since the fall of the Awami League, the question has resurfaced: Is a change in leadership on the horizon? How exactly will it happen, and who will step in?
Various people have attempted to answer these questions in different ways.
Many had assumed that the Awami League would be restructured around members against whom there were no allegations of serious crimes.
However, it became evident that even if a leader faced no such accusations at the time, the very moment they began the task of reorganizing the party, their name could be implicated in a case involving murder or “crimes against humanity.”
Yet, talk began circulating about a so-called “refined” or “reformed” Awami League. Names such as Saber Hossain Chowdhury, Shirin Sharmin Chaudhury, and even Narayanganj Mayor Selina Hayat Ivy were linked to this idea, although none of them publicly spoke of playing a role in restructuring the party.
However, one thing became clear: Regardless of the extent to which former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina bears responsibility for the Awami League’s current plight, in the eyes of the party’s grassroots activists, there is no leader other than her.
If the party were to be restructured under someone else’s leadership, it might remain a political party, but it would certainly cease to be the Awami League as they know it.
On the other hand, conversations with Awami League members, including former members of Parliament, over the past year or so suggest that if Sheikh Hasina herself were to initiate a transition process and select a successor, the rank and file might well accept that new leadership.
Yet there is another complication.
Over the last five decades, Bangladesh’s two major parties, the Awami League and the BNP, have become excessively dependent on particular families.
The BNP has never managed to step out of the shadow of its founder, Ziaur Rahman, nor has it made any serious attempt to do so.
The party is well aware that without the umbrella of the Zia family, its unity could crumble.
To keep the party together, leadership passed from General Zia to his wife, Khaleda Zia, and subsequently to their son, Tarique Rahman.
The situation within the Awami League is somewhat different.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not the party’s founder; the Awami League was established by Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani and Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy.
However, under Sheikh Mujib’s leadership, the Awami League became the embodiment of the hopes and aspirations of the Bengali people in what was then East Pakistan.
It was under Sheikh Mujib that the party spearheaded the movement for self-determination and contested the 1970 elections. He provided the direction for the independence movement in March 1971, and the subsequent Liberation War was fought in his name.
Because of this historical continuity, and the fact that Mujib and almost his entire family were killed on August 15, 1975, the Awami League became inextricably linked with the Sheikh family.
Despite the presence of prominent leaders within the party following Mujib’s assassination, they brought Sheikh Hasina back from exile in 1981 to take the helm.
It would come as no surprise if, during these difficult times for the Awami League, party leaders and activists once again looked towards the Sheikh family.
A parallel can be drawn with the BNP, where party members naturally accepted Khaleda Zia’s son, Tarique Rahman, as her successor.
Whether it is a matter of temporary responsibility or long-term succession, there is no doubt that the Awami League must contemplate its post-Hasina future.
At the same time, however, it must address how to regain public trust following 2024.
There appear to be two clear reasons for the party’s current organizational stagnation and crisis of morale.
First is the issue of leadership. Despite the continued faith in Sheikh Hasina, the Awami League is currently, effectively, leaderless.
Whether because of the ban on its activities, the imprisonment or flight abroad of many leaders, or the looming threat of legal cases hanging over many, the bottom line is that the party faces an acute leadership crisis.
Second, the Awami League has failed to come to terms with the events of 2024, even after two years. There appears to have been no internal self-criticism or even a meaningful process of introspection within the party.
Its leaders remain fixated on conspiracy theories and continue to deny their own culpability.
The Awami League needs to ask itself some critical questions:
Why did the movement to oust the government occur?
Why did a movement become necessary to bring about a change in government?
Why did students repeatedly take to the streets?
Why did the urban middle class support the movement?
Why did so many people lose their lives?
The answers to these questions will determine the message the party conveys to the public.
If the Awami League views itself as a party of the people, it must be accountable to them.
It is through this process of accountability that the party’s future leadership may become clear.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.

item.title: Gopalganj university library struggles with books, space, technology
item.description:
A shortage of academic and reference books, inadequate seating, slow internet and a lack of modern technological facilities are hampering study and research at the central library of Gopalganj Science and Technology University (GSTU).
The library, established in 2014, has 36,152 books, including academic publications, Liberation War-related books, fiction and novels. It also has around 1,500 printed journals and 500 magazines.
Despite the collection, students say the library lacks many course-specific and specialised books needed for their studies. It also does not have adequate access to international journals, e-books or modern digital facilities. An anti-plagiarism software system for teachers has yet to be introduced, while students do not have computers for academic use.
As a result, students say the library is yet to become an effective centre for higher education, research and knowledge practice.
A visit to the library found several air conditioners and fans out of order. There are also not enough desks for students, while chairs are placed so close together that users have to move them to get in and out. The movement creates noise that can be heard across the reading room, disrupting study.
Students have demanded high-speed internet, books according to their academic needs, a job corner and modernisation of the library.
Alamgir Hossain, a student of the 2018-19 academic session in the Department of Bangla, said around 9,320 students are currently studying at the university, while the library has seating capacity for only about 200.
“The student-to-seat ratio is around 1:50. There are not enough seats. Besides, the internet is slow and there is a shortage of necessary books. Noise from the surrounding areas also disrupts our studies,” he said.
Tamin Iqbal, a student of the 2019-20 academic session, said the library should serve as a centre for higher education, research and knowledge practice, but the existing facilities prevent it from playing that role.
“The number of students has increased, but the number of seats has not. The seating capacity must be increased. We also need high-speed internet. We hope the authorities will resolve these problems quickly,” he said.
Yaminur Rahman Arik, a student of the 2021-22 academic session, said the library lacked adequate subject-specific and reference books.
“Students come here to find books that are unavailable in the hall libraries, but often we cannot find them. There are also not enough reference books. The library does not provide enough scope for developing our knowledge and intellect through study,” he said.
“As a result, many students are frustrated and have become reluctant to use the library. We hope it will be turned into a proper centre for higher education, research and knowledge practice,” he added.
Acting Librarian Nasirul Islam said the library building has two floors, although it was originally planned as a four-storey facility.
“We are facing problems because of space and staff shortages. There is no automation system either, so we have to perform our work manually,” he said.
The library remains open from 9am to 10pm every day, he said, adding that staff members have to work in 13 shifts a week, putting additional pressure on them.
“Despite this, we are trying to provide the best possible services to students. The new vice-chancellor has discussed modernising and expanding the library with us and has assured us that he will work to resolve its problems,” Nasirul said.
Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Md Sohel Hasan, who was appointed on August 25, said he was aware of the problems facing the library.
“I have heard about the problems of the library. We will take initiatives to make it more up-to-date by adding reference books on various subjects, international research journals and reliable sources of information beyond textbooks,” he said.
“We want to create a library that will help teachers and students contribute more effectively to education and research. It will also be developed in a way that helps students prepare for competitive examinations, including the BCS,” the vice-chancellor added.

item.title: Boat race draws thousands to Titas River after two-year hiatus
item.description:
Thousands of spectators lined both banks of the Titas River in Brahmanbaria on Sunday as a colourful traditional boat race returned after a two-year hiatus.
Organised by the district administration, the race began at around 3:30pm along the stretch between Shimrailkandi and Medda areas of the district town.
Nine boats from different parts of Brahmanbaria took part in the competition, with the boat of Shapla Boys Club from Khamtapur village in Sadar upazila emerging as the winner.
Spectators began gathering along the riverbanks before noon, with the crowd swelling as the race drew closer. Once the competition began, cheers and chants from the packed riverbanks created a festive atmosphere.
The brightly decorated boats raced through the Titas as rowers paddled in unison, drawing loud cheers from supporters.
The last boat race on the Titas was held in 2023. The event is considered an important part of Brahmanbaria’s cultural heritage and traditionally attracts visitors from neighbouring districts.
Roni Alam, an expatriate living in Italy, travelled from Dhaka to watch the race.
“Boat racing is a festival close to our hearts. I came from Dhaka this morning despite the difficulties just to watch it. Seeing the enthusiasm of people on both banks has erased all my fatigue,” he said.
Another spectator, Al Amin Shaheen, said the event had created a festive atmosphere across the district.
“We want the boat race to be organised every year,” he said.
Brahmanbaria Deputy Commissioner Md Abusaid said the boat race was a popular traditional event.
“Boat racing is a festival close to the hearts of the people here. From next year, we will organise it on an even larger scale,” he said.
Brahmanbaria-3 MP Khaled Hossain Mahbub said the event highlighted the district’s cultural heritage amid what he described as recent negative campaigns about Brahmanbaria and its culture on social media.
“This boat race has shown that Brahmanbaria is a cultural capital. Boat racing is an integral part of our heritage,” he said, adding that he hoped the event would be organised regularly from next year.
Prizes were later handed over to the winning team at a ceremony attended by District Council Administrator Sirajul Islam, Deputy Director of the Local Government Division Shariful Islam, Superintendent of Police Shah Md Abdur Rouf, Additional Deputy Commissioner Ranjan Chandra Dey and other officials and local political leaders.

item.title: Fertiliser crunch fuels anger among Bhurungamari farmers
item.description:
Growing demand for fertiliser during the peak Aman season and ahead of early winter vegetable cultivation is fuelling frustration among farmers in Bhurungamari upazila of Kurigram, with many saying they are struggling to obtain supplies from authorised dealers.
The growing discontent has already spilled into protests, road blockades and incidents involving fertiliser dealers, reflecting mounting tensions over distribution.
Farmers also complain that they receive little field-level advice from agriculture officials on which fertiliser or pesticide to use, and in what quantities.
Agriculture officials, however, say there is no overall shortage of fertiliser in the upazila. They blame excessive use and stockpiling by some farmers for putting additional pressure on supplies.
A visit to several unions on Thursday found farmers moving from one sales outlet to another in search of fertiliser. Many said they either failed to get supplies or received much less than they needed.
At 9am, farmers were seen waiting at the BCIC dealer outlet of Messrs Janarddan Chandra Saha at Camp Mor in Bangasonahat Union. Three to five farmers were reportedly sharing one sack of DAP, while urea distribution had been suspended because of insufficient stock.
The farmers said their Aman paddy was around one-and-a-half to nearly two months old and they wanted to apply fertiliser to the fields. Agriculture officials, however, said DAP was not needed at this stage and applying it would be wasteful.
Mohammad Ali and Abdul Aziz, who had collected DAP, said they were unaware that the fertiliser was not recommended for Aman paddy at this stage.
“We do not know which fertiliser should be applied and when. We look at the condition of the plants and apply fertiliser accordingly,” Mohammad Ali said.
Abdul Aziz, who has two bighas of Aman, said he could not obtain urea and was therefore planning to use DAP instead.
“I do not know what else to do. I am using DAP because I could not get urea,” he said.
Abul Hashem, a representative of the dealer, said demand had increased sharply as farmers had begun cultivating eggplant on hundreds of bighas of land in the char areas.
“The demand for fertiliser is very high, but we are not getting enough to meet it,” he said.
In Gunaiyer Kuti char along the Dudhkumar River, farmers were cultivating early-season eggplant on hundreds of bighas of land.
Several farmers said they needed urea and DAP but could not obtain enough. They also complained that block supervisors, or BSs, rarely visit their fields to provide advice.
Instead, representatives of private agrochemical companies often visit the area, and farmers rely on their recommendations, they said.
Hridoy Molla, who has cultivated eggplant on four bighas, said he was unable to obtain fertiliser according to his requirements.
“I am mixing organic fertiliser and magnesium and applying them to the fields. The BSs do not come here. We apply fertiliser based on the condition of the plants,” he said.
Another farmer, Ramadan Ali, said he was also forced to rely on his own experience.
“We do not get fertiliser or advice. No BS comes here. We use our own knowledge to decide what fertiliser and pesticides to apply,” he said.
Kurigram Department of Agricultural Extension Deputy Director Abdullah Al Mamun denied that agriculture officials were disconnected from farmers, but acknowledged that staff shortages made it difficult to reach everyone.
“There is a tendency among farmers in Bhurungamari to apply excessive amounts of fertiliser. Many are seeking fertiliser even when it is not necessary and do not follow the recommended doses,” he said.
“There is no need to apply DAP to Aman paddy at this stage. Doing so would be a waste. After September 20, there will also be no need to apply urea. Many farmers use DAP instead of urea,” he added.
Regarding the farmers’ complaints about a lack of field-level advice, Mamun said BSs were required to visit fields and provide technical support through field days and other programmes.
“There are many farmers in each union, while we have a shortage of manpower. So it may not always be possible to reach everyone. However, BSs are stationed at every union parishad, and farmers can go there for advice whenever necessary,” he said.
Considering the increased demand, the agriculture department has sought an additional allocation of 300 tonnes each of urea and DAP for Bhurungamari, beyond the upazila’s regular allocation, Mamun said.

item.title: IGP: Police must enhance skills, capacity to combat cybercrime
item.description:
Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir on Sunday said there is no alternative to enhancing the skills and capacity of police personnel to combat cybercrime.
He made the remarks while inaugurating a 10-day Training of Trainers (ToT) course on investigation of cybercrime cases at the Police Staff College Bangladesh in Mirpur in Dhaka on Sunday.
“Artificial intelligence, deepfakes, encrypted communication systems and cloud computing have opened new avenues of opportunities, but at the same time created new challenges for law enforcement agencies,” the IGP said.
He said criminals are abusing technology to commit cyber-based fraud, online financial crimes, data theft, hacking, online harassment and digital extortion.
“Changes in the nature of policing have become a demand of the time to tackle the growing cybercrime. Developing investigation capacity to combat cybercrime is extremely essential for modern policing,” he said.
Addressing the police officers attending the training, the IGP said the course would help them acquire not only technical skills but also training and communication skills.
“The knowledge and skills gained through the training must be disseminated among other investigators,” he said, adding that effective training of other investigators would multiply the number of cybercrime case investigators.
The IGP thanked the Training Wing of Police Headquarters and the Police Staff College Bangladesh for arranging the timely training and stressed the need for regularly organising such training and updating training materials and modules.
Police Staff College Bangladesh Rector and Additional IGP Kazi Md Fazlul Karim presided over the programme, while CID chief and Additional IGP Barrister Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain attended as a special guest.
DIG (Training) Md Ekramul Habib delivered the welcome address, while Additional DIG (Training-2) Dr Mosammat Shehela Parveen presented the roadmap and implementation strategy for cybercrime investigation training.
Faculty members and resource persons of Police Staff College Bangladesh were also present.
The Police Staff College Bangladesh organised the 10-day course at the initiative of the Training Branch of Police Headquarters.
A total of 332 police officers participating in the ToT course will, in phases, provide training to field-level investigators of cybercrime cases.

item.title: ASK condemns alleged rape of two dancers hired for wedding event
item.description:
Two women dancers were allegedly gang-raped on the Titas River in Sarail, Brahmanbaria, after being hired to perform at a wedding, Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) said.
In a statement on Sunday, the rights group condemned the incident and expressed deep concern and outrage.
ASK said the two women were taken aboard a boat on September 11 on the pretext of performing at an event. They were allegedly held hostage at gunpoint and raped for an extended period.
The incident is a grave violation of the women’s safety and dignity and a serious assault on their professional rights and freedom to work, ASK said.
A woman has the fundamental right to pursue her chosen profession with dignity and work in a safe environment, it said. Working as a dancer or performing at an event for payment must not expose anyone to violence or abuse, ASK added.
The organisation said every citizen has the right to work safely, and ensuring such safety is the state’s responsibility.
ASK said the incident should not be viewed merely as a brutal crime committed by a few individuals. It also raises serious questions about the effectiveness of state mechanisms to prevent violence against women, law enforcement, and ensuring women’s safety while travelling and working. ASK demanded the immediate arrest of all those involved and their prosecution following an impartial and professional investigation. It also called for ensuring that no perpetrator escapes justice due to influence or pressure.
The organisation also demanded security, necessary medical treatment, psychological and legal support for the victims, as well as protection of their identities and privacy.
“Women’s safety is not merely a law-and-order issue; it is a question of equal rights, dignity and human rights,” ASK said, stressing that the state must ensure an environment where women can pursue their chosen professions without fear or insecurity.

item.title: All eyes on Nepal’s young ex-rapper prime minister after flood disaster
item.description:
He is the former rapper who rose to become Nepal’s prime minister with massive Gen Z support.
Now Balendra Shah and his new government are grappling with one of the worst disasters the country has seen.
The 36-year-old, popularly known as Balen, is the world’s youngest national leader and was elected just six months ago.
His ongoing response to the crisis that has killed at least 1,429 people and left another 5,651 people missing in Nepal and Tibet is being watched closely.
For some his government has not done enough.
Himal Thakur’s mother, father, older sister and older brother were working in Timure, Rasuwa district, when the flood hit.
He said he immediately asked the Nepal Army and local authorities for help, but “everyone I tried to ask for help seemed helpless”.
“I got no help from anywhere,” he told the ABC from Dhanusa district in Nepal.
Days later, his older sister’s employer, Machhapuchchhre Bank, secured a helicopter flight so he could search Timure himself.
Three of his family members are still missing, with the body of a man believed to be his brother found recently.
In March, the 23-year-old flew back from Cambodia, where he was working, to vote for Mr Shah’s party, the Rastriya Swatantra Party.
He said the government’s handling of the flood response made him “regret voting.”
“There is a lot more rescue and relief needed in the hill areas, but it hasn’t reached there. People haven’t received anything there yet. Most of the relief items seem to only reach as far as Nuwakot and not the epicenter of the flood,” he said.
The Nepal government was contacted for comment.
Nepal’s prime minister has experience with disaster recovery, using his structural engineering qualifications to help rebuild homes destroyed in the 2015 earthquake that killed nearly 9,000 people.
But this disaster is different, with Nepal’s army still rebuilding roads and installing pre-fabricated bridges supplied by India and China to reconnect communities.
Rescue teams and specialist equipment can only get into many places once access has been restored
In a frank admission, Bikram Timilsina, Nepal’s minister for information and communication, told DW that “on the very first day, we got a bit confused as to how to deal with the crisis.”
“[From the] second day onward, we have been putting all our efforts into swift search, rescue and relief works,” he said.
Parts of Sabin Shrestha’s childhood town Betrawati has been devastated by the floods.
He said the government mobilized the army, police and private helicopters as quickly as they could, but it should have been more open to outside help.
The Shah government initially believed its own authorities could respond to the disaster, declining offers of assistance from seven countries including China, the US and India, before later accepting them.
“At the end of the day, the question should not be who is providing the help. The question should be whether that help can save lives,” Mr Shrestha said.
Coordination between local governments and the central government could have been better, he said, with experienced community-based groups used to find people in remote areas.
Despite the scale of the crisis, Mr Shah has not given an address to the nation.
He waited a week to address Nepal’s parliament after the flood, but he posted daily to his millions of followers on Facebook, X and Instagram.
He shunned the mainstream media as a hip-hop artist rapping about corruption and inequality in Nepal, then as the independent mayor of Kathmandu and now as prime minister.
But relying on social media to communicate has seemingly not dampened support for his government.
More than 13 billion rupees ($123 million) has been donated to the prime minister’s disaster relief fund so far, something Kathmandu local Toran Pandit said was a sign the public trusted his government.
“His communication was grounded and empathetic — he treated the disaster like a shared national problem rather than just a localized issue, which clearly resonated because people and businesses immediately stepped forward to donate directly to the government’s relief fund,” he said.
“The way he managed the sheer scale of the situation on the ground, while also pivoting to stand up for Nepal on the global climate stage, really earns my respect. It makes me feel good about backing his team.”
Kathmandu local Sujata Sharma agreed.
“Having to deal with a catastrophic disaster like this within six months of the tenure could have been a disaster in itself,” she said.
Professor Krishna Shrestha, global development expert at the University of New South Wales, told the ABC that it was a unique moment in Nepali politics because there was “an outpouring of trust” in the national government.
“People are not really questioning whether this money will be spent and how it will be spent,” he said.
He said the reaction was very different to the 2015 earthquake, because of distrust in the political establishment and deep concerns about corruption.
But not all supporters are happy with Mr Shah’s style.
Last Tuesday marked one year since Nepali security forces opened fire on protesters in Kathmandu, killing 76 people.
Young people heavily backed Mr Shah in the first election after the uprising, believing in his anti-establishment and anti-corruption messages.
However, the prime minister did not attend Tuesday’s memorial, with other government ministers attending instead.
Pratish Shrestha represented injured protesters at the vigil and said the government could not forget them, or the promises they made about jobs, healthcare and transparency.
“The government is sitting in those chairs because of our blood, sweat and sacrifice,” the Kathmandu Post reported him as saying.
“Forgetting us is like cutting off your own roots.”
Professor Shrestha said not attending could be a sign of an inexperienced government, but ultimately Mr Shah’s response to the floods would define his prime ministership.
“At the moment, it is more gung-ho, this is the action-oriented leadership, regardless of what is happening in the public. I think this can make him isolated and increasingly seen negatively by the public down the track if it’s continued,” he said.
Mr Shah took to X mark his respects on Tuesday, saying that he hoped the anniversary would “inspire us all to move forward towards building a fair, transparent, and opportunity-filled Nepal.”
Several days after the flood, Himal Thakur received a call from a police officer telling him they had found his brother’s ID card on a body.
Mr Thakur could not identify the body, and the hospital would not release it because of questions over DNA test results, delaying Mr Thakur’s wish to give his brother traditional burial rites.
That was not his only concern.
“There are a lot of helpless people, including me. I have my younger sister, my brother’s son and my sister-in-law. I am still young and don’t feel grown up myself, so I have no idea how I am going to look after them,” he said.
“I can’t even expect too much from the government because I’m not sure how many people they can look after. There are so many people who need help.”

item.title: Sweden votes in election thriller, far right eyes govt role
item.description:
Sweden began voting Sunday in a general election after a tight race that will see either the far-right enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition reclaim power.
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8am (0600 GMT).
Clad in a pale blue suit, the 59-year-old who in 2021-2022 became the first woman to serve as Sweden’s prime minister voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Opinion polls have long credited the four parties in her left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats.
But the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take. Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats? Something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of cooperation?” Andersson told reporters after voting.
Her party, which governed the Scandinavian country for the better part of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest, has pledged to bolster the welfare state and help struggling households cope with rising costs.
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson has meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives now that his government’s clampdown on organized crime and immigration has begun to show results.
Deadly shootings and bombings by organized crime networks have decreased significantly in recent years, and asylum applications are at a record low.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people... to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing Donald Trump’s famous catchphrase.
His three-party minority coalition cut a deal in 2022 with the Sweden Democrats giving them influence over government policy, in particular on immigration and crime, in exchange for their support in parliament.
Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
It is now hoping to enter government. Kristersson has promised the far right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election.
“I think it’s a very important election this year, and hopefully a lot of people will realize that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society,” store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP as she voted at a polling station.
Ingrid Rudien, a 64-year-old assistant secretary, said she hoped the country “can unite together as a nation even though we may have a close result.”
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
“We’ve already won!” the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in Stockholm’s Kungsträdgården Park.
“Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish,” he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring “Make Sweden Sweden Again.”
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner attending the rally, told AFP she was voting for the far right.
“Like Jimmie, I want it to be like it was when I was young, in the old Sweden. I can’t cope with all this violence in society.”
Voting stations close at 8pm (1800 GMT) when exit polls were to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.
Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.
Around half of voters have cast their ballots in advance.
If the right wing were to win the election, the formation of a new government would be fairly straightforward.
But as the four left-wing parties are splintered ideologically, tough negotiations would be needed to form a government even if they hold a majority.

item.title: One dead, 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu
item.description:
At least one person was killed and 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the South Pacific nation’s government said on Sunday.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on Friday with more than 40 passengers and crew from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
Prime Minister Jotham Napat’s office said on Sunday morning that one dead body has been recovered, while 15 of those onboard have been “accounted for alive.”
The alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon when a diver working at a hotel on Santo saw a man floating in a life vest and pulled him to shore.
Hotel owner Ashley Beveridge told AFP he realized his employee was carrying a survivor from the missing boat, and someone in the restaurant alerted the authorities.
“He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours -- he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold,” Beveridge said in a telephone interview.
The survivor, Jeffson, said the boat sank on Friday morning.
“There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach -- lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area,” Beveridge said.
“He had gone all day and all night in the water.”
Beveridge said on Sunday afternoon: “At the last count it is 18 recovered and there is two or three dead so far.”
Cargo ship owners including a local politician, a local doctor with a plane and a private medical assistance vessel began their search on Saturday afternoon.
Survivors are being taken to the hospital on Santo Island, local media reported.
Napat’s office took over the maritime search on Sunday afternoon, after the prime minister earlier expressed frustration that he had been unable to reach senior officials.
In its Sunday statement, Napat’s office said “over 30 people remain missing at sea,” in addition to the one dead and the 15 “accounted for alive.”
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones. Search and rescue operations are continuing,” the statement read.
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
Beveridge, an Australian living in Vanuatu for eight years, said until Jeffson was discovered authorities had believed the ferry was adrift, and there was community frustration that the rescue effort took so long to get underway.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Noumea, New Caledonia said it is assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The center said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who took part in the search aboard his family’s cargo vessel, said two survivors and one body had been discovered Sunday on Tutuba Island.

item.title: Indonesia says six killed, 130 missing after ferry capsizes off Java
item.description:
Rescuers in Indonesia said at least six people were killed and 130 others were missing on Sunday after a ferry sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo was hit by bad weather and capsized.
The Virgo Transport 8, carrying 243 passengers and crew, had lost contact with its shipping company early on Sunday after departing from Surabaya in East Java.
Basarnas, Indonesia’s national search and rescue agency, said in its latest update that six people were killed and 130 were missing. It said 107 people had been rescued.
There were 213 passengers and 30 crew members on board, the agency added.
Indonesian Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the ship had capsized.
“From the information we received, based on helicopter surveillance... the ship capsized but has not sunk. As of 3pm (0700 GMT) it had not sunk yet, but it was capsized,” he said at a news conference in Banjarmasin.
Local search and rescue chief I Putu Sudayana earlier told AFP that the ship’s captain had reported to its owners before losing contact that the vessel was “tilting.”
Rescuers battled waves of up to 2.5 meters (8.2 feet) to reach the ferry, Sudayana told reporters.
“It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 meters long, is at great risk,” he said.
A Basarnas helicopter has joined the operation, he added.
The vessel’s last position had been detected in the Java Sea, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) from its destination.
Heri Purwanto, head of the Banjarmasin Sea Port Authority, said the ship, which was also carrying vehicles, lost contact at 2am on Sunday.
“We responded quickly to the incident report... Our main focus and top priority at this time is the safety of everyone on board the ship, and we are deploying a coordinated rescue operation,” Heri Purwanto said.
Rescue authorities have established a command center at the Banjarmasin port, with paramedics and ambulances on standby, an AFP reporter saw.
Dozens of relatives and friends of the passengers checked a whiteboard where the names of people rescued were being updated.
Jenah, 26, told AFP she came to the command post for information about her older brother.
“I am saddened and very shocked. Until now, I haven’t received any more information,” said Jenah, who like many Indonesians has only one name.
“He was travelling alone. I hope he survives. I couldn’t contact him since last night.”
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are the main reasons for the disasters.
On Monday, a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists working for local and international news agencies, went missing near a volcano, Mount Anak Krakatau, in Banten province. That search is ongoing.
The journalists were sent to cover the volcano’s eruption that paralyzed Jakarta’s main airport and several others.
Last month, a fire on board a ferry killed one person and left five others missing while 211 were rescued in the Lombok Strait off Indonesia’s Bali island.
The ferry had been heading from Bali to Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of August 12.
In July, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi.

item.title: TikTok, IDLC launch program to empower Bangladeshi SMEs
item.description:
TikTok on Sunday launched TikTok Bazaar, a nationwide capacity-building program designed to equip small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Bangladesh with the digital marketing skills and capabilities needed to grow their businesses locally and internationally.
Implemented in partnership with IDLC Finance, the country’s leading NBFI, TikTok Bazaar aims to support up to 2,500 SMEs across the country through a combination of in-person workshops, advanced training clusters, online mentoring, and ongoing virtual support.
The program will help entrepreneurs move beyond traditional social commerce by using TikTok to reach wider audiences, strengthen their brands, and explore new business opportunities locally and internationally.
Additionally, the partnership will help expand entrepreneurs’ access to practical digital skills and introduce participating businesses to a broader digital ecosystem.
TikTok Bazaar responds to a significant opportunity within Bangladesh’s developing digital commerce ecosystem.
Many local entrepreneurs already use social media to promote and sell clothing, food, cosmetics, personal care products, handicrafts, accessories and more.
However, they often lack access to structured, practical performance marketing training, limiting their ability to optimize campaigns and drive sustainable business growth.
The program will help participating businesses develop practical skills in TikTok campaign planning, creative content production, account configuration, advertising optimization, and performance measurement.
Businesses with operational readiness will also receive guidance on reaching overseas customers and building export-oriented campaigns.
Ferdous Mottakin, head of public policy and government relations, South Asia, TikTok, said: "Digital creativity can be a powerful driver of business growth. In partnership with IDLC, we aim to provide SMEs with the knowledge, tools and support they need to turn creativity into measurable commercial opportunity through TikTok Bazaar, whether they are serving customers locally or introducing Bangladeshi products to audiences overseas."
“Digital inclusion is no longer optional for today’s SME businesses, and if they are based outside the larger markets like Dhaka, or Chattogram this becomes even more critical for their growth. Bangladesh has a very potential SME scenario; and from IDLC, we are putting our best efforts to upskilling local SME business owners through collaborating with partners like TikTok,” said Adnan Rashid, head of SME, IDLC Finance.
Through TikTok Bazaar, TikTok aims to help Bangladeshi entrepreneurs build more resilient businesses, connect with new customers, and participate more fully in the digital economy.
The initiative will help SMEs build confidence, expand their reach and pursue sustainable growth in both domestic and international markets.

item.description:

The Bengal Tigresses will begin their 2026 Asian Games campaign against Asian powerhouse North Korea at Nagai Stadium in Osaka on Monday.
They will then face another Asian giant, South Korea, at the same venue in their second group-stage match.
The 20th edition of the continental multi-sport competition is being held in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, with football matches taking place across several Japanese cities.
The women’s football competition will be staged in Osaka, Fukuroi, Gifu and Kariya, while the men’s event will be played in Osaka, Toyota, Nagoya and Kariya.
At the last Asian Games in 2023, Japan won the women’s football gold medal in Hangzhou, while the Republic of Korea clinched the men’s title.
The 12-team women’s competition, divided into three groups, will run from September 14 to October 2. The men’s competition, featuring 15 teams following Iraq’s withdrawal, will take place from September 15 to October 3.
Bangladesh have been drawn in Group F alongside the Republic of Korea, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea and Myanmar.
The women in red and green, who made history by qualifying for the final round of the AFC Women’s Asian Cup 2026 in Australia in March, suffered an injury setback ahead of their Asian Games opener.

item.title: Standard Chartered Bangladesh hosts inaugural financial markets leadership forum
item.description:
Standard Chartered Bangladesh recently convened the inaugural Financial Markets Leadership Forum for Financial Institution clients in Bangladesh.
The event brought together regulators and nearly 200 industry leaders from banks, financial institutions, and capital markets to share perspectives on the evolving financial markets landscape, regulatory leadership, market stability, and opportunities for sustainable growth and innovation in Bangladesh.
Discussions during the forum focused on how stronger risk management practices, deeper and more liquid markets, and the strategic use of technology and sustainable finance can help Bangladesh navigate global uncertainty and capture new opportunities.
Participants highlighted the critical role of robust market infrastructure, regulatory clarity, and collaboration in strengthening Bangladesh’s position within the global financial system.
The forum was graced by Masud Khan, chairman of the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission as chief guest, and Md Sarwar Hossain, deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank, as special guest.
Their presence underscored the importance of close and continuous engagement between regulators and market participants in building a robust, resilient, and future ready financial system.
“Bangladesh’s financial markets stand at a pivotal moment,” said Enamul Huque, CEO, Standard Chartered Bangladesh.
“By deepening market liquidity, strengthening risk management, and embracing digital and sustainable finance, we can unlock the next phase of growth for our economy. Standard Chartered is proud to convene this dialogue and to stand alongside our regulators and clients as a long-term partner in building a more resilient, inclusive, and future ready financial system. My sincere thanks to Masud Khan, chairman of the BSEC as chief guest; Md Sarwar Hossain, deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank, as special guest; to all speakers, panelists, clients and colleagues for their valuable insights and participation.”
On behalf of Standard Chartered Bangladesh, the Bank's CEO, Enamul Haque, delivered the opening remarks and head of markets and corporate sales Sabah Saleheen Azim moderated the event and panel discussion.
Other panelists and speakers include Mashrur Arefin, managing director, City Bank PLC; Mehdi Zaman, DMD and head of treasury, offshore banking and financial institutions, Eastern Bank PLC; and from Standard Chartered, Ashish Malik, head, Markets FI Sales South Asia; Himanshu Dhyani, head of FI, GCNA, & Head of BBD, GCNA South Asia, CIB FI BBD; and Nasreen Rehman, head of financial institutions, Bangladesh.

item.title: 'The Difficult Bride' wins independent critics’ award at Venice
item.description:
Bangladeshi filmmaker Rubaiyat Hossain’s “The Difficult Bride” has won the Independent Film Critics Award, Premio Bisato d’Oro, at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival ahead of the festival’s official awards ceremony.
The recognition adds to a landmark year for the film, which made history as the first Bangladeshi feature to compete in the Orizzonti Competition at the Venice Film Festival.
Set in contemporary Dhaka, “The Difficult Bride” follows Zaineen, a young bride-to-be whose body begins to transform as she undergoes beauty rituals and preparations for her wedding.
Blending feminist folk horror, body horror, and supernatural elements, the film examines how women’s bodies can become sites of family expectations, social control, and desire.
Hossain said the award was particularly meaningful because of the personal themes explored in the film.
“I made ‘The Difficult Bride’ from a very intimate place, thinking about the ways women learn to inhabit, discipline, and sometimes fear their own bodies,” she said. “To have the film recognized by independent critics in Venice is deeply meaningful to me.”
She added that she hopes the film will allow audiences to experience Bangladesh beyond its social realities through its folklore, imagination, darkness, and beauty.
The Bisato d’Oro is an independent critics’ prize associated with the Venice Film Festival and is separate from the official awards presented by the Biennale.
The film’s Venice selection had already attracted international attention, with critics highlighting its use of South Asian wedding rituals within a feminist folk-horror framework. IndieWire described the film as transforming South Asian wedding tropes into “feminist folk horror."
Produced by Francois D’Artemare, “The Difficult Bride” is an international co-production between Bangladesh, France, Germany, Norway, and Portugal. International sales are handled by Films Boutique.

item.title: I Am Not My Grades: The Hidden Toll of the A-Level System
item.description:
Around the same time last year, I was the centre of attention for the whole family. Achieving eight A*s in my O Levels was a big deal, something most people never expected from me. Although I was a bit disappointed about the single A in Computer Science, I was happy enough seeing my parents, grandparents, and teachers genuinely proud and satisfied. I was the success story of the batch, operating on a high that made the future look limitless.
Now, I am the center of pity.
Teachers tilt their heads with sympathetic smiles in the corridors, and relatives offer soft, comforting words, treating my AS Level results like a sudden bereavement.
I got a B in Further Mathematics, which was, quite frankly, a humbling slap in the face.
That single grade didn't just hurt my pride; it paralyzed my entire future.
Right now, my peers are living in the exciting world of top-tier university applications. I watch as friends refine their personal statements, draft college essays, and register for entrance tests.
They are locking in their predicted grades and preparing to hit submit for the October 15 Oxbridge deadline, or aiming for Early Decision slots at elite US universities.
Last year, everyone assumed I would be the first in line for those forms.
Today, I can’t even open the application portals. I am completely locked out of the early cycle, unable to apply anywhere because my grades are temporarily stuck in limbo.
Instead of moving forward, my life has been thrown into reverse. I am currently trapped in the exhausting nightmare of preparing for an October retake.
Balancing the relentless demands of new A2 coursework while re-studying the grueling concepts of Further Math feels virtually impossible.
My daily routine has dissolved into a blur of past papers, sleepless nights, and a constant, quiet panic.
I am trying to keep my head above water in current classes while desperately trying to repair the past, leaving zero hours to breathe, let alone draft university essays.
To go from being the kid everyone brags about to the kid everyone tries to console is a jarring shift. High expectations create a narrow window for success; anything less than perfection gets treated like a total collapse.
The pity, while well-intentioned, stings worse than anger. It serves as a daily, painful reminder of where I was supposed to be versus where I am standing right now, watching everyone else sprint ahead while I am forced to pause.
Yet, sitting at my desk late at night surrounded by notes I thought I had already put behind me, I am coming to terms with a hard truth. O Levels were smooth sailing, but this period is forcing me to figure out what I am actually made of.
Falling short doesn't erase my past achievements, nor does a delayed application deadline mean a ruined life.
The October session is going to be brutal, and missing out on early applications hurts. But learning how to fight through burnout, rebuild from a set-back, and pull myself out of the center of pity is the most important lesson I will take into adulthood.
Avranil Saha is an A2 Level student at St. Francis Xavier's Greenherald International School, Dhaka.

item.title: Salahuddin, IRI delegation discuss cybercrime, online bullying
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Sunday held a meeting with a delegation of the International Republican Institute (IRI), with discussions focusing on preventing cybercrime and online bullying, and the proposed Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026.
The courtesy meeting took place at the minister's office at noon.
The delegation was led by IRI Resident Program Director John Fluharty. Helen Jerin Khan, MP, IRI Technical Adviser Ruksana Haque, and young politicians and IRI trainees Chamon Faria and Mohammad Prince were also present.
During the meeting, Fluharty briefed the minister on IRI's ongoing programs aimed at developing youth leadership and promoting violence-free political practices.
He said young people and political activists in Bangladesh are currently facing harassment and defamation due to cyberbullying and organized disinformation.
Fluharty called for a consensus-based policy and legal protection for both the government and opposition parties in this regard.
The minister assured the delegation that the government is aware of citizens' freedom of expression and personal security.
“Under Article 39 of the Constitution, every citizen has the right to express opinions and engage in constructive criticism, subject to reasonable restrictions. However, constructive criticism is not the same as character assassination or abusive language for political purposes,” he said.
Salahuddin said the government has been seeking opinions from the international community, media personalities, senior editors and civil society stakeholders for the past two months as part of efforts to revise the proposed Cyber Security (Amendment) Act.
He said the main objectives of the law is to restore civility in the digital space, protect women and young people from cyberbullying and ensure professional protection for journalists while preventing any misuse of the law.
The minister said the government will welcome constructive recommendations from both international and local stakeholders to strengthen digital security and establish a violence-free political environment.
Additional Home Secretary (Political and Immigration Wings) Dr Ziauddin Ahmed and Joint Secretary of the Political-1 Branch Rebeka Khan, among others, attended the meeting.

item.title: Chief prosecutor: Threats to witnesses cannot obstruct tribunal proceedings
item.description:
International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam has said no one will be allowed to threaten or intimidate witnesses in crimes against humanity cases or obstruct judicial proceedings.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at his office on Sunday afternoon.
Asked about allegations that witnesses were being threatened by the accused in a crimes against humanity case over incidents in Chittagong, Aminul said he had received complaints in this regard.
He said law enforcement agencies had been instructed to take necessary measures to ensure the witnesses’ security.
“If there is evidence that anyone is threatening a witness in a case, legal action can be taken,” he said.
He, however, said threats and intimidation would not be allowed to disrupt the judicial process.
“No investigation or trial before this tribunal can be obstructed through intimidation or threats,” the chief prosecutor said. On a complaint filed by the family seeking justice for the murder of journalist couple Sagar Sarwar and Meherun Runi, Aminul said the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) was currently investigating the case.
He said Megh’s maternal uncle Roman had submitted a written application to the tribunal seeking its intervention.
“Their expectation is that we will also investigate the case or assist the PBI if we receive any information,” he said, adding that the application would be reviewed.
“If the matter does not fall under a widespread or systematic offence, we will inform them accordingly,” Aminul said.
He said anyone had the right to submit an application to the tribunal and that the family had exercised that right.
“The PBI investigation is ongoing. At this point, we consider the Sagar-Runi incident an individual murder case. We will examine whether it falls within the scope of a widespread or systematic offence,” he said.
He added that the application had been accepted, although it was not a matter of formally registering a case at this stage.

FBL-ESP-LIGA-LEVANTE-BARCELONA

Lamine Yamal struck twice to help Barcelona to an exciting 4-2 win at Levante on Sunday in La Liga, extending the Catalans' perfect start to the season.

Hansi Flick's side reestablished their three point lead over Real Madrid at the top of the table, after Los Blancos beat Rayo Vallecano on Saturday.

Xavi Espart opened the scoring for the champions in Valencia with Yamal netting the second and then scoring a penalty early in the second half.

Barca may have a 100 percent record so far from their five games but their defensive frailties were exposed as Ivan Romero and Roger Brugue pulled Levante back into the game in the final stages.

Substitute Karim Adeyemi made the game safe for Barca in stoppage time with a stunning solo goal, breaking through at pace and beating Mathew Ryan.

"It was not our best game of course. We had a great start. In the second half we struggled a little bit," Flick told reporters.

"We have to fight to improve. It's normal, we have situations we have to make better, much better. We'll tell the team and go on to the next match, but with the result I'm happy."

Barcelona defender Eric Garcia said that the team relaxed a bit in the second half and it nearly cost them.

"It was a hard game, we did make it harder for ourselves than it needed to be," Garcia told Movistar.

"But it has to teach us something -- if you give any opponent a bit of breathing room they get on top of you."

The Catalans came flying out of the blocks at the Cituat de Valencia stadium, where Levante were unbeaten in eight matches prior.

The visitors took the lead in the fifth minute, with Levante barely touching the ball before Barca defender Espart found the net.

Barca cut through the middle of Levante's team too easily and the 19-year-old finished from the edge of the box with the help of a slight deflection.

It was Espart's first goal for the club, with the young midfielder brought into the first team this season by Flick and deployed at left-back.

Levante responded with a spell of concerted pressure and Barca were fortunate to maintain their advantage.

Petar Ratkov could not get a proper shot away when well placed and Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia saved well from Brugue.

Levante soon came to regret those spurned chances when Raphinha created Barca's second for teenage star Yamal.

The Brazilian rounded goalkeeper Ryan and squared for Yamal to smash into the empty net in the 19th minute.

Between the afternoon summer heat and some heavy tackles, the pace of the game slowed.

Paying the penalty

Yamal claimed his second goal soon after the restart, winning and then converting a penalty.

The Spain winger was hacked down by Aissa Mandi and powered the resulting spot kick past Ryan for his seventh goal in four games across all competitions.

Levante could have pulled one back but Andreas Christensen cleared Romero's bobbling shot off the line.

The striker did get on the scoresheet when Espart gave the ball away with a loose pass towards Christensen, and Romero nipped in to strike.

Levante fans roared when Brugue capitalised on a Marc Bernal error, with Garcia saving his first shot but the striker able to nudge home the rebound.

However, former Borussia Dortmund winger Adeyemi ended the hosts' dreams of a point with a dynamic burst through the defence and then a cool finish to match.

Barcelona host promoted side Racing Santander on Wednesday, while Levante welcome Athletic Bilbao.

Earlier on Sunday, Celta Vigo were held to a 1-1 home draw by Malaga. Later, Diego Simeone's Atletico Madrid visit Real Sociedad and Getafe face Deportivo La Coruna.
